newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma soil moisture levels continue to fall.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma soil moisture levels continue to fall.

text.p: The following is a weekly crop summary from the Oklahoma Agricultural Statistics Service for the week ended August 3.

Hot, dry weather prevailed across most of the state, causing moisture levels to spiral downward. Both topsoil and subsoil moisture supplies were at their lowest level of the year. Dry weather permitted farmers and ranchers 6.5 days of fieldwork, the highest of the year.

WHEAT: Seedbeds were prepared for planting in many areas of the state, particularly in the West Central and Southwest districts where fields were more than 30 percent prepared. Moisture is needed for good soil tillage.
CORN: Condition improved in the Panhandle district where moisture was received. The crop was entering the maturity stage across the southern tier of Oklahoma.

SORGHUM AND SOYBEANS: Condition remained roughly the same as last week. Moths were observed in grain sorghum in the North Central district causing concern for developing eggs and potential worm problems. Soybean maturity continues to be reported in the Southwest district.

COTTON AND PEANUTS: Dry weather has reduced condition rating slightly. Dryland crops are in need of moisture. Spraying has started in some Southwest district cotton fields for worms and weevils. Peanuts have not yet reached the maturity stage of development.
PASTURE AND RANGE: Condition has started to decrease because of the lack of rain. Native ranges are beginning to turn brown in many counties.
Tame grass production was slowed due to the shortage of moisture. Some protein supplementation was occurring on dried-down pastures in the South Central district.

CATTLE: Marketings remained mostly average. Feeder steer prices averaged $82 per cwt, down a little more than $1 from last week. Feeder heifers averaged $79.50 per cwt, down nearly 80 cents. Insect activity was heavy in a few southern and eastern counties.

COUNTY SPOTLIGHT: Woods County (NC) - Crops and pastures need rain. Bryan County (SC) - Spotty rains this week helped dryland crops in some

areas but missed others. Hay crop may be short if we don't get more general rains soon. Cattle marketings light - prices at local markets on beef cattle remaining very strong. Older cows still being culled. Some protein supplementation occuring on dried-down pastures.
WEATHER FOR WEEK ENDING SUNDAY, AUGUST 3, 1997 - Temperatures averaged 77.6 degrees Northeast district to 82.7 degrees Southwest district.

Individual Mesonet stations ranged from 58.4 degrees at Vinita, Seiling, and Miami to 104.6 degrees at Walters. Precipitation averaged 0.19 in. South Central to 1.05 in. Panhandle. Individual Mesonet stations ranged from 0.00 in. at several stations to 3.62 in. at Hooker. Soil temperatures ranged from 69.8 degrees at Miami to 107.0 degrees at McAlester, Cheyenne, and Idabel.
